card.title: Angle Bisector Between Two Lines — The a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ Rule

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Angle bisectors are the equal-distance locus made algebraic: normalise each line into a signed distance, equate up to ±, and the two equations fall out — perpendicular to each other by an identity, not a coincidence. The a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ rule classifies acute versus obtuse, but only after the constants-positive convention pins the normals' directions; the origin-side corollary rides the same convention.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
(a₁x+b₁y+c₁)/√(a₁²+b₁²) = ±(a₂x+b₂y+c₂)/√(a₂²+b₂²)
c₁, c₂ > 0 and a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ < 0 ⟹ (+) bisector is acute

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: NEB-style practice beyond the verified PYQs recorded on the parent canonicals.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Standardise the constants first; the rule is sign-convention-dependent.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The convention's teeth*** - the same two lines with one equation multiplied by -1 flip the rule's verdict - the constants-positive convention is what makes a1a2 + b1b2 decisive.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The bisector definition is the equal-distance locus; the +- pair is the absolute value's two sign arrangements.  ·  Normalise: (ax+by+c)/sqrt(a^2+b^2) is the signed distance. Bisectors: normalised forms equal up to +-; the pair is always perpendicular. Convention first: make c1, c2 > 0; then a1a2 + b1b2 < 0 => (+) bisector is acute, > 0 => obtuse. Origin side: constants positive, take (+). The rule is the dot product of the normal vectors read as wedge geometry.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Angle Bisector Rule a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ This canonical carries the **angle-bisector machinery**: normalised distance equations, the sign convention, the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ acute/obtuse rule, and the built-in perpendicularity check. The bisectors of two lines are the locus of points equidistant from both — one definition, two equations, one sign decision.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror - **Normalised distance:** dividing aᵢx + bᵢy + cᵢ by √(aᵢ² + bᵢ²) turns the line's equation into "signed distance = 0"; its absolute value at any point is the true distance to the line. - **Bisector equations:** (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/√(a₁² + b₁²) = ±(a₂x + b₂y + c₂)/√(a₂² + b₂²) — the (+) and (−) pair, always perpendicular to each other.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Check c1, c2 > 0 before computing a1a2 + b1b2 - one glance, one avoided wrong verdict.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (5m): Write the equations of the bisectors of the angles between the lines x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 2x + y − 3 = 0.** — **Normalisers:** √5 and √5 (both lines have the same √(a²+b²) — a happy accident). **Bisector pair:** (x + 2y − 5)/√5 = ±(2x + y − 3)/√5 ⟹ x + 2y − 5 = ±(2x + y − 3).…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): Find the bisectors of x + y − 1 = 0 and x − y − 1 = 0 and determine which contains the origin.** — **Standardise:** c₁ = −1 < 0 ⟹ rewrite L₁ as −x − y + 1 = 0; c₂ = −1 < 0 ⟹ L₂ as −x + y + 1 = 0. Now both constants positive. **Normalisers:** both √2. **Bisector pair:** (−x−y+1)/√2 = ±(−x+y+1)/√2.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Verify with the perpendicularity check: the two bisectors' slopes must multiply to -1.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The two angle bisectors are perpendicular for every pair of intersecting lines.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (6m): For the lines 3x + 4y − 5 = 0 and 5x + 12y − 13 = 0, find the acute angle bisector.** — **Standardise:** c₁ = −5 < 0 ⟹ rewrite L₁: −3x − 4y + 5 = 0; L₂: c₂ = −13 < 0 ⟹ −5x − 12y + 13 = 0. **Normalisers:** 5 and 13.…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): Show that the two bisectors of any two intersecting lines are perpendicular, using their equations.** — **Setup:** bisectors B₊: (N₁ = N₂) and B₋: (N₁ = −N₂) where Nᵢ = (aᵢx+bᵢy+cᵢ)/√(aᵢ²+bᵢ²) are the normalised forms.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — Bisectors as an Equal-Distance Locus - The defining idea: points equidistant from two lines. Normalising converts each line's equation into a signed distance, and "distance₁ = distance₂" is exactly the ± pair — the absolute values create two equations because "equal magnitude" admits two sign arrangements.…  ·  ## 4. Deep Conceptual — Why the Constants' Signs Must Be Standardised First - The a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ rule is **not sign-invariant**: multiplying one equation by −1 flips both the constants and the rule's verdict. The convention "make c₁, c₂ > 0 first" pins the normal vectors' directions so the rule's statement is unambiguous — the rule without the convention is a coin flip.…  ·  ## 5. Worked Example Types - **Type A — write the bisector pair:** normalise, present ±, done. - **Type B — classify acute/obtuse:** standardise constants, compute a₁a₂ + b₁b₂, assign. - **Type C — origin-side selection:** constants positive, (+) sign. - **Type D — perpendicularity check:** slopes multiply to −1 as the built-in audit.
